Checkpoint saved the conversation as it went, so the job could carry on.

captions.text: Today's black box: MCP, the way agents use tools they don't own.
Let's open it. But first, a tool that's stuck.
search_handbook is a Python function. Call it inside this program, and it works.
Then a second program in another folder tries to import it. Predict: what happens?
ModuleNotFoundError. The only way in is a Python call, so no other agent can use it.
Here's a server in plain Python, with no library. Read a line, work out a reply, write a line.
It isn't complete. But that's what an MCP server is: a program that reads and writes lines.
See flush=True? Without it, the reply can sit in a buffer. Remember that.
Send tools/list as one line of JSON. One line comes back, with the same id, listing the tool.
The client is plain Python too. Popen starts the server as its own program.
readline can wait for ever, so a timer kills a server that goes quiet.
And that's the whole trick: write a line, flush it, read a line.
Now the real thing, with the official SDK. MCPServer makes a server, and @mcp.tool() adds a tool.
It's a normal function. The name, the docstring and the type hints become the tool. No async.
Predict: does the same by_hand.py work, with no changes?
It does. The same line went out, and a real server answered.
The client didn't change, and that's the point of a protocol. The SDK built this schema.
Now tools/call, from a program that never imports whitebox.
The same handbook text, and whitebox isn't loaded here. The tool is unlocked.
Now break it. Five bad requests, each on a new connection. Which ones can the model read?
A protocol error means no tool ran. A tool error is a normal result, with isError set.
The ValueError's message never left the server. Only ToolError's message gets through.
Now the error worth remembering. A first request with no _meta, then a perfect one. Predict.
Refused. The first request set the protocol, and this connection is locked into the old one.
Even a harmless ping does it, and the ping itself succeeded, so nothing warned you.
The reverse fails too. The fix is a new connection, with _meta from the very first request.
That lock exists because there are two protocols, and older servers speak only the older one.
The new opening has no handshake. Every request carries _meta, and discover is optional.
The old opening is a handshake: initialize, then a notification. A v2 server answers both.
An older server refuses discover, the connection survives, and the handshake works.
Two things have versions here. 2026-07-28 is a protocol. 2.3.0 is a Python library that speaks it.
Library v2 renamed FastMCP to MCPServer. Tutorials from before v2 show the older name.
Library 1.30.0 speaks only the handshake. Say which one you mean: the rules, or the package.
Why go stateless? Run a remote server as two copies behind a balancer. This demo is pretend.
A remembered session lives in one copy's memory. Predict: what happens on the other copy?
It fails. But self-contained requests work on either copy, and that's why _meta is on every one.
Sticky routing piles work onto one copy. The traffic is made up, to show the shape.
A restart wipes sessions. A shared store works, and it's one more service to run.
Stateless doesn't mean your app has no state. A handle is an ordinary argument, passed on each call.
Two real copies take turns. With baskets in memory, copy B has never heard of the handle.
In a shared file, either copy can serve any call. The handle must point at something shared.
On stdio, stdout is the protocol's pipe. So what does a print in a tool do? Five runs each.
On v2, a plain print arrived after the reply, flushed went to stderr, and every call was answered.
On v1, a flushed print landed before the reply. It still got an answer here.
But 20,000 lines glued the reply onto a half-written line: 0 of 5 answered. Log to stderr.
Your turn. Open exercises.py and complete the five TODOs.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.

captions.text: A server is a program that reads and writes lines. The SDK does the rules for you.
The protocol stopped holding state, so your application holds it. On local stdio, little changes.
We tested Python SDK servers on one Mac. Test yours.
